91	## Post 2: "A Pattern for Scaling the Value Proposition of LLMs: Ensemble and Distil" (2024-02-06)
92	
93	Source: `/Users/neelanpather/dev/cybernaut_mini/docs/blog-archive/ensemble-and-distil.md` — Author: Stuart Reid (interns Moabi Mokhoro, Deon van Heerden)
94	
95	### 1. WHAT IT IS
96	
97	A knowledge-distillation pattern ("ensemble and distil") for scaling LLM labeling capability to big corpora: curate a representative dataset, label it with multiple LLMs, greedily ensemble them into a teacher that beats any single model (90.4% human agreement vs Unicorn's 83.6%), then distill the teacher into ordinary-least-squares regressions over off-the-shelf sentence-transformer embeddings. The punchline: an OLS student on `sentence-t5-large` embeddings (80.40% agreement with teacher) beats GPT-4 (79.90%) at sentiment classification while costing ~$0 marginal and running ~100× faster. Solves the "$92,000 and 57 compute-days for 10M stories" problem from the previous post. Five-step pattern: Curate → Label → Ensemble → Distil → Scale.
98	
99	### 2. ARCHITECTURE
100	
101	1. **Curate** — the 10,378-story dataset (all years/industries/categories) from the previous post. (This post says 10,378; the previous post says 10,368 — minor source inconsistency.)
102	2. **Label** — each story labeled by the full model zoo (18 label columns: TextBlob-0.10/0.20/0.30, VADER-0.10/0.20/0.30, Flair-0.50/0.75/0.95, Sigma, FinBERT, FinBERT-Tone, Text-Bison, Text-Unicorn, Gemini-Pro, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4-Original), each producing labels in {−1, 0, +1}.
103	3. **Ensemble (Teacher)** — greedy "iterative addition": start with best model, iteratively add the most "additive" model (one that improves ensemble accuracy) until none help. Teacher score = raw **sum** of member labels: `Teacher = Unicorn + GPT-3.5 + GPT-4-Original + Sigma + Bison`. Discretization: sum ≥ 1 → Positive; ≤ −1 → Negative; else Neutral.
104	4. **Overfitting check** — rerun iterative addition 1,000 times on data samples to get a probability distribution over the possible best ensembles.
105	5. **Textbook (features)** — encode each story as `f"{Headline}. {Description}"` with each of 35 sentence-transformer models.
106	6. **Distil (Students)** — `sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` fit on embeddings (X) → continuous teacher sum score (y). 75/25 train/test split (`train_test_split(test_size=0.25, random_state=42)`).
107	7. **Predict + threshold** — regression output thresholded identically (≥1 → +1, ≤−1 → −1, else 0); metric = out-of-sample 3-class exact-agreement with the discretized teacher.
108	8. **Scale** — deploy the winning student (embeddings + linear model) over the full corpus.
109	
110	### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS
111	
112	**Ensemble construction (iterative addition trace):**
113	- Start `Unicorn` (83.6%) → +`GPT-3.5` (+2.80%) → +`GPT-4` (+2.00%) → +`SigmaFSA` (+1.60%) → +`Bison` (+0.40%).
114	- Final teacher: **90.4%** agreement with human labels — 6% absolute above Unicorn alone.
115	- Stars-alignment conditions for ensembling: members better than random; correlated when right; uncorrelated when wrong. (Boosting does this explicitly by training on errors.)
116	- Stability test: across 1,000 simulations, this ensemble was best 51% of the time; same-minus-Bison best 13.8%; same-plus-TextBlob-0.30 best 11%.
117	- Teacher aggregation formula (from code): `ensemble_score = Text-Unicorn + GPT-3.5-Turbo + GPT-4-Original + Sigma + Text-Bison` (each member label ∈ {−1,0,+1}, so sum ∈ [−5, +5]).
118	- Discretization (code): `classes[score <= -1] = -1; classes[score >= 1] = 1; else 0`.
119	
120	**Student setup:**
121	- All students are OLS `LinearRegression` (sklearn); fitted on embedding vectors → continuous Teacher sum; predictions thresholded at ±1.
122	- Input sentence: `"{Headline}. {Description}"`.
123	- 38 models in the survey total: teacher + 7 LLMs + 30 OLS students. (The code lists 35 sentence-transformer names; small internal inconsistency.)
124	- Split: `test_size=0.25, random_state=42`; accuracy measured out-of-sample vs teacher classes.
125	
126	**Sentence transformers evaluated (full list from code, fastest→slowest):** `TaylorAI/bge-micro-v2`, `TaylorAI/bge-micro`, `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `all-MiniLM-L6-v1`, `TaylorAI/gte-tiny`, `all-MiniLM-L12-v2`, `all-MiniLM-L12-v1`, `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-small`, `intfloat/e5-small-v2`, `intfloat/e5-small-unsupervised`, `all-distilroberta-v1`, `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-base`, `intfloat/e5-base-v2`, `intfloat/e5-base-unsupervised`, `mukaj/fin-mpnet-base`, `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `all-mpnet-base-v1`, `sentence-t5-base`, `gtr-t5-base`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`, `paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2`, `distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v1`, `distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v2`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-base`, `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`, `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-large`, `intfloat/e5-large-v2`, `intfloat/e5-large-unsupervised`, `sentence-t5-large`, `gtr-t5-large`, `all-roberta-large-v1`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large`.
127	
128	**Results (out-of-sample agreement with Teacher):**
129	- LLM reference targets: PaLM-2 Unicorn 89.04%; GPT-4 Original 79.90%.
130	- 384-dim: best `e5-small-v2` 76.54%; fastest & most popular `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` 68.13%.
131	- 768-dim: best `sentence-t5-large` (listed in this bucket) **80.40%** 🏆; fastest `all-distilroberta-v1` 73.34%; most popular `all-mpnet-base-v2` 75.46%.
132	- 1024-dim: best `e5-large-v2` **80.21%** 🏆; fastest & most popular `bge-large-en-v1.5` 76.58%.
133	- Multilingual: best `paraphrase-multilingual-base-v2` 78.63%; fastest `multilingual-e5-small` 72.99%; most popular `distil-use-multilingual-cased-v2` 69.21%.
134	- Two students beat GPT-4 (79.90%): `sentence-t5-large` (80.40%) and `e5-large-v2` (80.21%).
135	- E5 family "punches above weight": best <100M params = `e5-small-v2`; best 100–200M = `e5-base-v2`; best 300–400M = `e5-large-v2`. Unsupervised E5 variants nearly identical to supervised. They chose `multilingual-e5-large` going forward. Cited paper: "Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training" (Wang et al., arXiv 2212.03533).
136	
137	**Economics:**
138	- GPT-4 labeling 10M stories: **$92,000**; student: $0.00 marginal ("could buy three Nvidia H100's" with the savings).
139	- GPT-4: ~0.5 s/story → 57 compute-days for 10M. Student: ~0.005 s/story → <1 compute-day for 10M.
140	- Whole analysis: 198 lines of Python. Libraries: `sentence_transformers`, `sklearn` (LinearRegression, train_test_split), `numpy`, `pandas`, `json`, `datetime`.
141	- Result tables report: model type, HF likes, HF downloads, out-of-sample accuracy vs Teacher; per-model code records parameter count (`sum(p.numel())`), encode runtime, dimensionality, accuracy → `Results.csv`.
142	
143	**Pattern reuse (8 downstream tasks named):** Sentiment (Pos/Neu/Neg); Tense (Past/Present/Future); News category (M&A, Legal, Results…); Brand Safety (Safe/Unsafe); Beat (Opinion/Formal/Investigative); Political Bias (Left/Centrist/Right); Statement (Forward/Backward looking); IAB Website Classification (700+ categories). Used jointly with Alphix Solutions.
144	
145	**Data files (format from code):** `small/nosible-news-small.json` (dict keyed by story, with Headline/Description), `small/nosible-news-small-labels.json` (dict of per-model labels per story). Superseded by HF dataset `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` (100k samples).
146	
147	### 4. BUILD RECIPE (educational scale)
148	
149	1. Take the labeled dataset from Post 1's recipe (or `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` from HF) with ≥3 independent LLM/classic labelers per row, labels mapped to {−1,0,+1}. [disclosed]
150	2. Implement iterative addition: greedily grow an ensemble starting from the single best model by human agreement, adding whichever remaining model maximizes ensemble accuracy (ensemble score = sum of member labels, thresholded at ±1), stopping when no addition helps. [disclosed]
151	3. Bootstrap-resample and rerun iterative addition ~1,000 times; keep the ensemble that wins most often. [disclosed]
152	4. Compute the continuous Teacher score per row as the raw sum of member labels; keep both the sum (regression target) and the ±1-thresholded class. [disclosed — exact code given]
153	5. For each candidate sentence-transformer, encode `"{Headline}. {Description}"` with `SentenceTransformer.encode`; record parameter count, encode runtime, and dimensionality. [disclosed — exact code given]
154	6. Split 75/25 (`random_state=42`); fit `LinearRegression(embeddings → Teacher sum)`; predict on test; threshold predictions at ±1; score 3-class exact-match vs the thresholded Teacher on the test set. [disclosed — exact code given]
155	7. Tabulate all students and raw LLMs on the same test split; pick the best accuracy/speed trade-off (expect T5/E5-large-class winners). [disclosed]
156	8. Deploy: batch-embed the full corpus and apply the linear model; optionally export the linear head as a single matrix-vector product fused after the encoder (e.g., ONNX). [inferred — deployment mechanics unstated; assumed standard embedding + dot-product serving]
157	9. Educational shrink: use 3–5 cheap API models as ensemble members and ~5 small sentence-transformers (bge-micro, MiniLM, e5-small-v2, e5-base-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2) to keep runtime minutes-scale. [inferred — scale reduction assumption]
158	
159	### 5. GAPS
160	
161	- The image-only result tables (full per-model accuracy/likes/downloads for all ~35 students) are not in text; only category winners quoted.
162	- The human-agreement measurement for the ensemble (which 250-row subset, how the 1,000 simulations sampled data) is under-specified.
163	- Why the ensemble uses an unweighted sum (no learned weights/calibration) is not justified; no per-class metrics (precision/recall/confusion) reported anywhere.
164	- Hardware used for the 0.005 s/story student timing is unstated.
165	- `paraphrase-multilingual-base-v2` (winner name in multilingual table) doesn't exactly match any model in the code list (closest: `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`) — likely a typo the replicator must resolve.
166	- The 30-vs-35 student count and 10,368-vs-10,378 record count inconsistencies are unresolved.
167	- The raw label JSON files are no longer downloadable (superseded by the HF dataset, which has a different schema).
168	
169	---
170	
171	## Post 3: "Matching GPT-5.1 at Financial Sentiment with Active Learning and Qwen3" (2025-12-12)
172	
173	Source: `/Users/neelanpather/dev/cybernaut_mini/docs/blog-archive/fast-enough-to-matter-productionizing-tiny-transformers-for-signal-extraction.md` — Author: Simon van Dyk (team: Matthew Dicks, Simon van Dyk, Gareth Warburton, Stuart Reid)
174	
175	### 1. WHAT IT IS
176	
177	The production-grade evolution of ensemble-and-distil: three fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B causal-LM text classifiers (financial sentiment; forward-looking detection; prediction detection) trained on 100,000 real-world web texts labeled by an 8-LLM majority-vote ensemble and refined via an active-learning relabeling loop with GPT-5.1 as oracle. The sentiment model hits **87.34% accuracy on real-world data** and **86.4% on Financial PhraseBank**, beating FinBERT on both and matching GPT-5.1 at orders-of-magnitude lower cost/latency. Classification is framed as next-token prediction (no classification head). Models and datasets are open-sourced on HuggingFace under the NOSIBLE org; signals feed NOSIBLE Search Feeds ("web-scale surveillance") for aspect-based sentiment analysis.
178	
179	### 2. ARCHITECTURE
180	
181	1. **Data sampling** — sample a Search Feed of financial news from the NOSIBLE index; real-world, messy, varied snippets (their variety is deliberate — forces robust patterns over memorized artifacts).
182	2. **Step 1: Look at your data** — hand-label 200 uniformly sampled texts (negative/neutral/positive); study ambiguity and class balance; oversample under-represented classes (they needed more negatives). Hand-labeled set kept separate from the LLM-labeled set.
183	3. **Step 2: LLM ensemble labeling** — unambiguous decision-tree prompt (full prompts for all three tasks disclosed verbatim); 8 LLMs each label every text; **majority vote** produces the label. Prompt validated first against the 200 hand labels; disagreements + LLM rationales drive prompt refinement (e.g., discovered earnings reports mislabeled neutral → emphasized financial materiality over tone). Then scale 200 → 10,000 → 100,000 samples. Data shape evolution: (200,1) text → (200,2) +human_label → (10,000,9) 8 LLM label columns → (10,000,10) +majority_vote.
184	4. **Step 3: Baseline classifiers** — embed texts with 6 embedding models (via OpenRouter, embeddings memoized to .npy); train linear `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=0.00001)` per embedding; 80/20 train/val split (pre-shuffled, subscript split); target mapping {0: neutral, 1: positive, −1: negative}. Baseline confirms signal, label quality, and gives a benchmark. Scaling to 100k added 1–2% accuracy. Baseline: 86.65% train / 85.93% val (20,000 val samples).
185	5. **Step 4: Active-learning relabeling loop** — (a) find rows where ALL linear models agree with each other but DISAGREE with the majority-vote label; (b) consult oracle GPT-5.1 (prompt disclosed: given the labeling prompt + the linear models' consensus prediction, oracle returns `{"correct": true/false, "label": ..., "reason": ...}`); (c) relabel if oracle sides with the baselines, else keep; (d) drop the worst-performing linear model (on val) from the ensemble each iteration; (e) retrain and repeat until no new disagreements. Result: +3.38% train (→90.03%), +3.55% val (→89.48%). Final dataset reached "iter_18" (`financial_sentiment_100.0k_iter_18.ipc`).
186	6. **Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B** — classification as next-token prediction: chat-templated prompt (system: "Classify the financial sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral."; user: text; assistant target: label + `<|im_end|>`); label masking (−100 on prompt tokens); left-padding; EOS excluded from metrics; monitor train/val loss and PhraseBank accuracy during training. Candidates tested: ModernBERT, DeBERTa, several causal LLMs — Qwen3-0.6B won.
187	7. **Evaluation** — vs FinBERT (`ProsusAI/finbert` via HF Trainer, macro-F1 + accuracy) and vs zero-shot frontier LLMs, on (a) Financial PhraseBank (4,840 expert-labeled snippets, Malo et al. 2014 — "fake news"/contrived) and (b) the 20% held-out real-world validation set; plus accuracy-vs-cost frontier plots.
188	8. **Serving** — HF Inference Endpoints, SGLang engine on an L40S GPU; OpenAI-compatible client with `temperature=0, max_tokens=1, logprobs=True, top_logprobs=3`, regex-constrained decoding `"(positive|neutral|negative)"`, `enable_thinking: False`; logprobs → per-label confidence via `math.exp(logprob)`.
189	
190	### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS
191	
192	**Headline numbers:**
193	- 87.34% accuracy on real-world data; 86.4% on Financial PhraseBank; beats FinBERT on both; matches GPT-5.1 accuracy; GPT-5.1 topped it "by a margin" on the benchmark but is orders of magnitude more expensive.
194	- Baseline linear model: 86.65% train / 85.93% val → after relabeling 90.03% / 89.48% (+3.38 / +3.55). "~3.5% validation accuracy improvement as a result of relabeling."
195	- 100,000-sample dataset; 20,000 validation samples (80/20).
196	
197	**Labeler ensemble (8 models, via OpenRouter):** xAI Grok 4 Fast; Grok 4 Fast (reasoning enabled); Google Gemini 2.5 Flash; OpenAI GPT-5 Nano; OpenAI GPT-4.1 Mini; OpenAI gpt-oss-120b; Meta Llama 4 Maverick; Qwen Qwen3 32B. Aggregation = majority vote.
198	
199	**Embedding ensemble (6 models, via OpenRouter):** Qwen3-Embedding-8B; Qwen3-Embedding-4B; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; OpenAI Text-Embedding-3-Large; Google Gemini-Embedding-001; Mistral-Embed-2312. (Usage volume put NOSIBLE 2nd on the OpenRouter embeddings leaderboard for Qwen3-Embedding-8B, expected 1st once operationalized.)
200	
201	**Baseline classifier:** `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=0.00001)`; labels {positive:1, neutral:0, negative:−1}; polars DataFrames; embeddings cached as .npy; confusion matrices computed per split.
202	
203	**Oracle:** OpenAI GPT-5.1 via OpenRouter. Oracle prompt embeds the original labeling prompt as the user message and asks in the system message whether the baseline-consensus label is correct, returning JSON `{"correct": "true"|"false", "label": <one of labels>, "reason": ...}` (ends with "P.S. Think fast there is no time to waste.").
204	
205	**Prompts (all three disclosed verbatim in post — key properties):**
206	- Sentiment: negative/neutral/positive defined via *material impact* on financial performance, share price, reputation, or outlook; materiality note enumerates share price, revenue, costs, profitability, cash flow, guidance, regulatory exposure, reputation, risk exposure, competitive position; explicit ASCII decision tree (check clearly-negative → clearly-positive → else neutral); conflicting sentiment → pick dominant, else neutral; JSON output `{"rationale", "financial_sentiment"}`; default-to-neutral instruction.
207	- Forward-looking: classify main event's temporal orientation "forward" | "not-forward"; disambiguation rules: ignore reporting-verb tense; plans/intentions/targets/guidance = forward even if approved in past ("Board approved new product launch" → forward); when in doubt → not-forward; JSON `{"tense", "rationale"}`.
208	- Prediction: "predictive" | "not-predictive"; predictive = concrete claim/forecast/estimate about a specific event; numerical estimates about current or future stats = predictive; analyst estimates/ratings predictive even in past tense; plans/hopes/schedules/retrospectives = not-predictive; default not-predictive; JSON `{"rationale", "causal"}`.
209	
210	**Fine-tuning setup (full script disclosed):**
211	- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` (600M params; "run it on a phone"; not hosted on OpenRouter). Alternatives tested: ModernBERT, DeBERTa, several causal LLMs.
212	- Approach cites Qwen3Guard (arXiv 2510.14276) "Guard approach" — classification as next-token prediction, no classification head; representation is the tokenized text directly (not embeddings).
213	- Tokenization: `apply_chat_template(..., add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False)`; answer = `f"{label}<|im_end|>"`; `assert len(answer_tokens)==2` (label must be a single token + EOS); truncate at 2048 tokens.
214	- Label masking: `labels = [-100] * len(prompt_tokens["input_ids"]) + answer_tokens["input_ids"]` — loss only on label+EOS tokens ("forces the model to learn classification, not memorize prompts").
215	- Left padding: `tokenizer.padding_side = "left"`; `pad_token = eos_token` if missing; `trust_remote_code=True` ("essential for Qwen3"). Right-padding "breaks everything" for causal batched prediction.
216	- Model load: `torch.bfloat16`, `device_map="auto"`.
217	- TrainingArguments: `gradient_accumulation_steps=4`, `per_device_train_batch_size=16`, `per_device_eval_batch_size=16`, `num_train_epochs=5`, `learning_rate=2e-5`, `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `warmup_ratio=0.03`, `max_grad_norm=1.0`, `weight_decay=0.1`, `neftune_noise_alpha=5`, `bf16=True`, `optim="adamw_torch_fused"`, `group_by_length=True`, `torch_compile=False`, `eval_strategy="steps"`, `eval_steps=500`, `save_steps=500`, `save_total_limit=3`, `load_best_model_at_end=True`, `metric_for_best_model="eval_val_loss"`, `logging_steps=10`, `logging_first_step=True`, `report_to="none"`.
218	- Eval sets during training: 5% of train, the 20% val split, and Financial PhraseBank; collator `DataCollatorForSeq2Seq(padding=True)`; `num_proc=8` for tokenization.
219	- Metric pitfall (disclosed bug): including EOS tokens in accuracy gave "suspiciously good results"; fix = mask both −100 and `<|im_end|>` token id (`compute_metrics_without_eos`: shift preds `[:, :-1]` vs labels `[:, 1:]`, `valid_mask = (labels != -100) & (labels != eos_token_id)`, macro-F1 + accuracy); `preprocess_logits_for_metrics` argmaxes logits (Batch, Seq, Vocab) → (Batch, Seq) to save memory. Verified true accuracy after training on an out-of-sample dataset.
220	- Data files: `financial_sentiment_100.0k_iter_18.ipc` (polars IPC), `financial_phrase_bank.ndjson`; workspace `/workspace/.nosible`; `train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42)`.
221	- FinBERT eval: `ProsusAI/finbert`, label2id {positive:0, negative:1, neutral:2}, max_length 512, eval batch 32, macro-F1 preferred.
222	
223	**Benchmarks/eval sets:**
224	- Financial PhraseBank: 4,840 snippets, human-expert labeled, Malo et al. (2014) — characterized as contrived/"fake news"; FinBERT does well here but "sucks on real-world data" (overfit to cleaner benchmark data).
225	- Real-world eval: held-out 20% of the 100k NOSIBLE dataset ("real news").
226	
227	**Cost methodology (disclosed):**
228	- LLMs: input+output token cost per million summed in a **10:1 input:output ratio** (typical for the labeling prompt).
229	- Fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B: estimated at a conservative **100:1 ratio** (output = label token + EOS only).
230	
231	**Serving recipe (disclosed):** HF Inference Endpoints → Deploy → HF Inference Endpoints; hardware "a beefy GPU like a L40S"; engine SGLang with Max Prefill Tokens 65536; container args `--dtype float16 --cuda-graph-max-bs 128 --disable-radix-cache`; Download Pattern "Download Everything". Client: OpenAI SDK, `temperature=0`, `max_tokens=1`, `logprobs=True`, `top_logprobs=len(labels)`, `extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, "regex": "(positive|neutral|negative)"}`; confidence = `math.exp(lp.logprob)` per label token. Key insight: "causal models aren't just for text generation" — logprobs make them production-ready classifiers.
232	
233	**Open-sourced artifacts (HF):** datasets `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` (100k cleaned/deduped/labeled), `NOSIBLE/forward-looking`, `NOSIBLE/prediction`; models `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment-v1.1-base`, `NOSIBLE/forward-looking-v1.2-base`, `NOSIBLE/prediction-v1.1-base`.
234	
235	**Citations:** FinBERT (Araci 2019, arXiv 1908.10063); Financial PhraseBank (Malo et al. 2014; HF `takala/financial_phrasebank`); Qwen3 Technical Report (arXiv 2505.09388); Qwen3Guard Technical Report (arXiv 2510.14276).
236	
237	### 4. BUILD RECIPE (educational scale)
238	
239	1. Gather 1k–10k real-world financial text snippets (mix polished earnings prose with noisy consumer/off-topic text — the variety is deliberate). [disclosed principle; inferred source — use RSS/news APIs or the released `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` dataset directly]
240	2. Hand-label 200 uniform samples as negative/neutral/positive; note ambiguity patterns and class balance; oversample scarce classes (negatives). Keep this set held out. [disclosed]
241	3. Write a decision-tree labeling prompt with domain definitions, materiality note, disambiguation rules, default-to-neutral fallback, and JSON-only output — or reuse the verbatim prompts from the post. [disclosed]
242	4. Label the full set with 3–8 cheap API LLMs (post used 8 via OpenRouter); take majority vote; validate against the 200 hand labels; refine prompt from disagreements + rationales. [disclosed; inferred that 3–5 labelers suffice at educational scale]
243	5. Embed all texts with 2–6 embedding models (post: Qwen3-Embedding family, text-embedding-3-large, gemini-embedding-001, mistral-embed; educationally, local sentence-transformers work); cache embeddings to .npy. [disclosed; inferred local-model substitution]
244	6. Train one `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=1e-5)` per embedding, 80/20 split; check train≈val accuracy (no overfit) and that accuracy beats chance (signal exists). [disclosed — code given]
245	7. Active-learning loop: find rows where all linear models agree but the majority vote disagrees → ask an oracle LLM (post: GPT-5.1; any strong model works) with the disclosed oracle prompt → relabel when oracle sides with baselines → drop worst linear model on val → retrain → repeat to convergence (post took ~18 iterations). [disclosed; inferred oracle substitution]
246	8. Fine-tune `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` with the disclosed script: chat template (system instruction + text + assistant label), label masking (−100 on prompt), left padding, single-token label + `<|im_end|>`, bf16, lr 2e-5 cosine, 5 epochs, batch 16 × grad-accum 4, neftune 5, weight decay 0.1, best-model-on-val-loss. [disclosed — full hyperparameters given]
247	9. Evaluate with the EOS-excluded token metric (mask −100 AND eos id) on val + Financial PhraseBank (`takala/financial_phrasebank` on HF); compare against `ProsusAI/finbert` and one or two zero-shot API LLMs with the same labeling prompt; verify on an out-of-sample set. [disclosed]
248	10. Serve with regex-constrained single-token decoding (`max_tokens=1`, regex `(positive|neutral|negative)`, thinking disabled) and read logprobs for calibrated confidence — via SGLang/vLLM on GPU, or plain `transformers` generation at toy scale. [disclosed serving config; inferred that local transformers/ONNX inference is an acceptable educational stand-in for the L40S/SGLang endpoint]
249	11. Optional: repeat the whole pipeline for the forward-looking and prediction binary tasks using the two other disclosed prompts. [disclosed]
250	
251	### 5. GAPS
252	
253	- Chart-only numbers: the PhraseBank and real-world accuracy figures for every compared LLM/FinBERT, and the actual dollar costs on the cost-vs-accuracy plots, are images — only 87.34%, 86.4%, and the baseline/relabeling numbers appear in text.
254	- How ModernBERT/DeBERTa/other causal candidates scored (why exactly Qwen3-0.6B won) — no comparison numbers given.
255	- How the raw Search Feed was sampled/filtered (query, dedup, date range, per-company balance) and how negatives were oversampled — proprietary pipeline.
256	- Exact number of relabeled samples per iteration, total relabeled count, and total iterations (only inferable as ~18 from the filename `iter_18`).
257	- Which/how many linear models remained at convergence after the drop-worst rule.
258	- Fine-tuning hardware, wall-clock time, and training cost are unstated (only the `/workspace` path hints at a rented GPU box).
259	- Production throughput/latency numbers for the served Qwen3-0.6B (only "orders of magnitude" cheaper/faster claims and the 100:1 cost-ratio estimate).
260	- Tie-breaking rule for the 8-model majority vote (8 is even; 3-class ties possible) is not specified.
261	- The `embed_data()` helper (OpenRouter embedding calls) is referenced but not shown.
262	
263	---
264	
265	## Cross-Post Synthesis (for the replica build guide)
266	
267	The three posts form one evolving pattern, each stage a drop-in upgrade of the last:
268	
269	| Dimension | Post 1 (2024-01) | Post 2 (2024-02) | Post 3 (2025-12) |
270	|---|---|---|---|
271	| Role | Benchmark + label source selection | Ensemble teacher + linear distillation | LLM-labeled + active learning + causal-LM fine-tune |
272	| Labelers | 12+ individual models | 5-member summed ensemble (90.4% human agreement) | 8-LLM majority vote + GPT-5.1 oracle relabeling |
273	| Student | — | OLS on sentence-transformer embeddings (80.4%) | Fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B next-token classifier (87.3% real-world) |
274	| Ensemble rule | — | greedy iterative addition, sum, threshold ±1 | majority vote; drop-worst baseline pruning |
275	| Key metric | agreement with 250 human labels | OOS agreement with teacher (75/25 split, seed 42) | accuracy/macro-F1 on 20% holdout + PhraseBank, EOS-excluded |
276	| Cost story | $0.00983/story GPT-4; $92k/10M | ~$0 marginal; 0.005 s/story; <1 compute-day/10M | 100:1 vs 10:1 token-ratio cost model; L40S + SGLang |
277	
278	An educational replica (cybernaut_mini-style) can implement all three stages against one small corpus: Stage A = multi-model labeling + agreement matrix (Post 1), Stage B = iterative-addition teacher + OLS students (Post 2), Stage C = active-learning relabel loop + Qwen3-0.6B fine-tune with label masking and regex-constrained serving (Post 3). Every load-bearing formula, prompt, and hyperparameter needed is quoted above; the main unavoidable substitutions are the news corpus itself and the retired 2023-era LLMs (PaLM-2 Bison/Unicorn, GPT-4-Original).

# NOSIBLE Blog Archive: Clean-Room Reverse-Engineering Notes

Educational replica notes covering three posts from the NOSIBLE technical blog, in chronological order (the 2024 posts form a two-part series that the 2025 post supersedes).

---

## Post 1: "News Sentiment Showdown: Who Checks Vibes Best?" (2024-01-28)

Source: `/Users/neelanpather/dev/cybernaut_mini/docs/blog-archive/news-sentiment-showdown-who-checks-vibes-best.md` — Author: Stuart Reid

### 1. WHAT IT IS

A benchmark study answering "how can financial-news sentiment be quantified?" It compares 12+ sentiment classifiers — spanning lexicon models (TextBlob, VADER), pre-LLM transformers (Flair, FinBERT, FinBERT-Tone, SigmaFSA), and cloud LLMs (GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, PaLM-2 Bison/Unicorn, Gemini-Pro) — against 250 hand-labeled news stories and a representative 10,368-story corpus subset. The problem it solves: identifying which model best matches human sentiment judgment on real financial news, and quantifying the cost of using cloud LLMs at corpus scale (10M stories). It sets up the distillation post that follows.

### 2. ARCHITECTURE

1. **Corpus filtering** — SQL query over the NOSIBLE news index ("engine" table) run in a nested for-loop over (year × category × industry), selecting the top stories by `media_coverage` per intersection.
2. **Dataset carving** — three tiers: `nosible-news-small` (10,368 records; biggest 1 story per intersection), `nosible-news-medium` (22,422; biggest 3), `nosible-news-large` (43,324; biggest 5). "Biggest" = most widely covered by independent publishers simultaneously (proxy for impact/realness).
3. **Hand-labeling** — 250 randomly chosen stories labeled by humans (Positive/Neutral/Negative) as ground truth.
4. **Model inference** — every model labels the stories; LLMs all receive the identical few-shot prompt with zero modifications; input text is headline + description.
5. **Evaluation** — pairwise agreement matrices: (a) all models vs. human labels on the 250 hand-labeled set (rows/cols ordered by human agreement), (b) all models vs. each other on the 10,368-story small set (ordered by agreement with Text-Bison, the best on that set).
6. **Cost analysis** — average cost per story labeled per cloud LLM, extrapolated to 10M stories.

### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS

**Dataset construction:**
- Representation constraints: news from all years 2014–2023, all 30 Nosible news categories, all 145 industries.
- Quality filters (verbatim from SQL): `source_language_rank>=0.50`, `source_variance_rank>=0.50`, `accepted=true`, `apex_story=true`, `source_is_banned=false`, `media_coverage>=3`, `title_num_words>=5 AND <=25`, `description_num_words>=10 AND <=50`, `ORDER BY media_coverage DESC LIMIT 10` per (year, category, industry) cell.
- Note: prose says "description between 5 and 50 words" but the SQL says `>=10` — SQL is authoritative.
- Dataset fields: Headline, Description (lede/SEO description), Category, Company, Sector (GICS), Industry (GICS), Continent, Country.
- 250 hand-labeled stories chosen at random; authors admit internal disagreement on several labels.

**Models evaluated (with thresholds):**
- Random baseline: −1/0/+1 with equal probability (useful for post-test probabilities).
- TextBlob [2013]: lexicon polarity, thresholds 0.15 / 0.30 / 0.45.
- VADER [2014]: lexicon+rules compound score, 3 thresholds (results reference VADER-0.10, -0.20, -0.30).
- Flair [2019]: distilBERT-based, binary POS/NEG; converted to 3-class by accepting the top label only if probability crossed a confidence threshold — tested at 70%, 80%, 90%.
- FinBERT [2019]: `ProsusAI/finbert` on Hugging Face.
- SigmaFSA [2022]: `Sigma/financial-sentiment-analysis` on Hugging Face (appears to be fine-tuned Financial BERT, not FinBERT).
- FinBERT-Tone [2023]: `yiyanghkust/finbert-tone` on Hugging Face.
- GPT-3.5-Turbo [2022]: accessed via LangChain.
- Text-Bison [2023]: PaLM 2, via Google Cloud Platform, default hyperparameters.
- Text-Unicorn [2023]: largest PaLM 2 model, via GCP, default hyperparameters.
- GPT-4 [2023]: via OpenAI API.
- GPT-4-Turbo [2023]: specifically `gpt-4-1106-preview`.
- Gemini-Pro [2023]: via Google Cloud (nano and ultra unavailable to them).

**Prompt (few-shot, identical for all LLMs):** system framing "You are a sentiment classification AI"; constrained to reply only POS/NEU/NEG; "When you are unsure of the sentiment, you MUST reply with NEU"; exactly 9 few-shot examples (3 POS, 3 NEU, 3 NEG, covering product demand, market/jobs numbers, and FDA/pharma scenarios); ends with `Story: {story}\nReply:`. Full prompt text is disclosed verbatim in the post.

**Results (agreement with human labels):**
- Text-Unicorn (PaLM-2): 84% — 1st place.
- GPT-4: 74% — 2nd place; 8% higher than GPT-4-Turbo (so GPT-4-Turbo ≈ 66%).
- FinBERT: ~69% ("better off using FinBERT than GPT-3.5"; agrees with Unicorn the same amount as GPT-3.5).
- FinBERT-Tone: agreed with Unicorn only 53% vs FinBERT's 69% — a regression.
- VADER (0.10 threshold): agreed with Unicorn 56% of the time; TextBlob "very nearly random."
- Gemini-Pro beat Bison (same pricing model; they'd choose Gemini-Pro). Speculation that Gemini-Ultra would beat Unicorn.
- Flair, SigmaFSA, FinBERT-Tone did not outperform VADER despite higher compute cost — attributed to overfitting to their training domains.

**Cost/speed:**
- GPT-4 average cost per story: $0.00983; GPT-4-Turbo: $0.00329 (GPT-4-Turbo 2.98× cheaper).
- VADER is 339× faster than FinBERT — "may still have a place in real-time trading environments."
- 10M-story extrapolation shown in bar chart (the $92,000 GPT-4 total is stated in the follow-up post).
- The NOSIBLE corpus already exceeded 10M documents at time of writing.

**Other labeling tasks named (pattern generalizes):** Sentiment; Forward-Looking vs backward; Category (M&A, charitable donation, etc.); Political Bias; Journalistic Beat.

**Downloads:** original 2024 export superseded by the `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` HF dataset (100,000 cleaned, deduplicated, labeled samples).

### 4. BUILD RECIPE (educational scale)

1. Assemble a corpus of financial news headlines+descriptions (a few thousand rows from an open dataset or synthetic sample). [inferred — replica lacks the NOSIBLE index; assume any diverse financial news source]
2. Stratify sampling across year × category × industry cells, taking top-N per cell by a "coverage" proxy; apply the quality filters (title 5–25 words, description 10–50 words, dedup). [disclosed — SQL given; the coverage metric must be approximated, e.g., by story duplication count]
3. Hand-label ~250 random stories as {−1, 0, +1}. [disclosed]
4. Implement classifiers: TextBlob and VADER with 3 thresholds each; Flair with 70/80/90% confidence gating for the neutral class; `ProsusAI/finbert`, `yiyanghkust/finbert-tone`, `Sigma/financial-sentiment-analysis` via `transformers`. [disclosed]
5. Implement LLM labeling with the exact few-shot prompt from the post (POS/NEU/NEG, default-to-NEU rule, 9 examples), using any modern API models as stand-ins for PaLM-2/GPT-4. [disclosed prompt; inferred model substitution]
6. Compute the pairwise agreement matrix (percent exact 3-class label match) across all models plus humans; order rows by human agreement. [disclosed]
7. Record per-story cost and latency per API model; extrapolate to a large-corpus cost figure. [disclosed protocol; use current pricing]
8. Add a random-label baseline for post-test probability computation. [disclosed]

### 5. GAPS

- The 250 human labels and the labeling rubric/guidelines the humans used are not published.
- Exact agreement-matrix numbers exist only as images; only a handful of cells are quoted in prose.
- API hyperparameters (temperature, max tokens) for the LLM calls are unstated ("defaults" for PaLM only).
- How ties/refusals/malformed LLM outputs were handled is not described.
- The precise definition/computation of `media_coverage`, `source_language_rank`, `source_variance_rank`, `apex_story`, and the 30-category/145-industry taxonomies are proprietary.
- Latency measurement methodology (the 339× VADER-vs-FinBERT claim) is not detailed.

---

## Post 2: "A Pattern for Scaling the Value Proposition of LLMs: Ensemble and Distil" (2024-02-06)

Source: `/Users/neelanpather/dev/cybernaut_mini/docs/blog-archive/ensemble-and-distil.md` — Author: Stuart Reid (interns Moabi Mokhoro, Deon van Heerden)

### 1. WHAT IT IS

A knowledge-distillation pattern ("ensemble and distil") for scaling LLM labeling capability to big corpora: curate a representative dataset, label it with multiple LLMs, greedily ensemble them into a teacher that beats any single model (90.4% human agreement vs Unicorn's 83.6%), then distill the teacher into ordinary-least-squares regressions over off-the-shelf sentence-transformer embeddings. The punchline: an OLS student on `sentence-t5-large` embeddings (80.40% agreement with teacher) beats GPT-4 (79.90%) at sentiment classification while costing ~$0 marginal and running ~100× faster. Solves the "$92,000 and 57 compute-days for 10M stories" problem from the previous post. Five-step pattern: Curate → Label → Ensemble → Distil → Scale.

### 2. ARCHITECTURE

1. **Curate** — the 10,378-story dataset (all years/industries/categories) from the previous post. (This post says 10,378; the previous post says 10,368 — minor source inconsistency.)
2. **Label** — each story labeled by the full model zoo (18 label columns: TextBlob-0.10/0.20/0.30, VADER-0.10/0.20/0.30, Flair-0.50/0.75/0.95, Sigma, FinBERT, FinBERT-Tone, Text-Bison, Text-Unicorn, Gemini-Pro, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4-Original), each producing labels in {−1, 0, +1}.
3. **Ensemble (Teacher)** — greedy "iterative addition": start with best model, iteratively add the most "additive" model (one that improves ensemble accuracy) until none help. Teacher score = raw **sum** of member labels: `Teacher = Unicorn + GPT-3.5 + GPT-4-Original + Sigma + Bison`. Discretization: sum ≥ 1 → Positive; ≤ −1 → Negative; else Neutral.
4. **Overfitting check** — rerun iterative addition 1,000 times on data samples to get a probability distribution over the possible best ensembles.
5. **Textbook (features)** — encode each story as `f"{Headline}. {Description}"` with each of 35 sentence-transformer models.
6. **Distil (Students)** — `sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` fit on embeddings (X) → continuous teacher sum score (y). 75/25 train/test split (`train_test_split(test_size=0.25, random_state=42)`).
7. **Predict + threshold** — regression output thresholded identically (≥1 → +1, ≤−1 → −1, else 0); metric = out-of-sample 3-class exact-agreement with the discretized teacher.
8. **Scale** — deploy the winning student (embeddings + linear model) over the full corpus.

### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS

**Ensemble construction (iterative addition trace):**
- Start `Unicorn` (83.6%) → +`GPT-3.5` (+2.80%) → +`GPT-4` (+2.00%) → +`SigmaFSA` (+1.60%) → +`Bison` (+0.40%).
- Final teacher: **90.4%** agreement with human labels — 6% absolute above Unicorn alone.
- Stars-alignment conditions for ensembling: members better than random; correlated when right; uncorrelated when wrong. (Boosting does this explicitly by training on errors.)
- Stability test: across 1,000 simulations, this ensemble was best 51% of the time; same-minus-Bison best 13.8%; same-plus-TextBlob-0.30 best 11%.
- Teacher aggregation formula (from code): `ensemble_score = Text-Unicorn + GPT-3.5-Turbo + GPT-4-Original + Sigma + Text-Bison` (each member label ∈ {−1,0,+1}, so sum ∈ [−5, +5]).
- Discretization (code): `classes[score <= -1] = -1; classes[score >= 1] = 1; else 0`.

**Student setup:**
- All students are OLS `LinearRegression` (sklearn); fitted on embedding vectors → continuous Teacher sum; predictions thresholded at ±1.
- Input sentence: `"{Headline}. {Description}"`.
- 38 models in the survey total: teacher + 7 LLMs + 30 OLS students. (The code lists 35 sentence-transformer names; small internal inconsistency.)
- Split: `test_size=0.25, random_state=42`; accuracy measured out-of-sample vs teacher classes.

**Sentence transformers evaluated (full list from code, fastest→slowest):** `TaylorAI/bge-micro-v2`, `TaylorAI/bge-micro`, `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `all-MiniLM-L6-v1`, `TaylorAI/gte-tiny`, `all-MiniLM-L12-v2`, `all-MiniLM-L12-v1`, `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-small`, `intfloat/e5-small-v2`, `intfloat/e5-small-unsupervised`, `all-distilroberta-v1`, `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-base`, `intfloat/e5-base-v2`, `intfloat/e5-base-unsupervised`, `mukaj/fin-mpnet-base`, `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `all-mpnet-base-v1`, `sentence-t5-base`, `gtr-t5-base`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`, `paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2`, `distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v1`, `distiluse-base-multilingual-cased-v2`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-base`, `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`, `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5`, `thenlper/gte-large`, `intfloat/e5-large-v2`, `intfloat/e5-large-unsupervised`, `sentence-t5-large`, `gtr-t5-large`, `all-roberta-large-v1`, `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large`.

**Results (out-of-sample agreement with Teacher):**
- LLM reference targets: PaLM-2 Unicorn 89.04%; GPT-4 Original 79.90%.
- 384-dim: best `e5-small-v2` 76.54%; fastest & most popular `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` 68.13%.
- 768-dim: best `sentence-t5-large` (listed in this bucket) **80.40%** 🏆; fastest `all-distilroberta-v1` 73.34%; most popular `all-mpnet-base-v2` 75.46%.
- 1024-dim: best `e5-large-v2` **80.21%** 🏆; fastest & most popular `bge-large-en-v1.5` 76.58%.
- Multilingual: best `paraphrase-multilingual-base-v2` 78.63%; fastest `multilingual-e5-small` 72.99%; most popular `distil-use-multilingual-cased-v2` 69.21%.
- Two students beat GPT-4 (79.90%): `sentence-t5-large` (80.40%) and `e5-large-v2` (80.21%).
- E5 family "punches above weight": best <100M params = `e5-small-v2`; best 100–200M = `e5-base-v2`; best 300–400M = `e5-large-v2`. Unsupervised E5 variants nearly identical to supervised. They chose `multilingual-e5-large` going forward. Cited paper: "Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training" (Wang et al., arXiv 2212.03533).

**Economics:**
- GPT-4 labeling 10M stories: **$92,000**; student: $0.00 marginal ("could buy three Nvidia H100's" with the savings).
- GPT-4: ~0.5 s/story → 57 compute-days for 10M. Student: ~0.005 s/story → <1 compute-day for 10M.
- Whole analysis: 198 lines of Python. Libraries: `sentence_transformers`, `sklearn` (LinearRegression, train_test_split), `numpy`, `pandas`, `json`, `datetime`.

## Post 3: "Matching GPT-5.1 at Financial Sentiment with Active Learning and Qwen3" (2025-12-12)

Source: `/Users/neelanpather/dev/cybernaut_mini/docs/blog-archive/fast-enough-to-matter-productionizing-tiny-transformers-for-signal-extraction.md` — Author: Simon van Dyk (team: Matthew Dicks, Simon van Dyk, Gareth Warburton, Stuart Reid)

### 1. WHAT IT IS

The production-grade evolution of ensemble-and-distil: three fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B causal-LM text classifiers (financial sentiment; forward-looking detection; prediction detection) trained on 100,000 real-world web texts labeled by an 8-LLM majority-vote ensemble and refined via an active-learning relabeling loop with GPT-5.1 as oracle. The sentiment model hits **87.34% accuracy on real-world data** and **86.4% on Financial PhraseBank**, beating FinBERT on both and matching GPT-5.1 at orders-of-magnitude lower cost/latency. Classification is framed as next-token prediction (no classification head). Models and datasets are open-sourced on HuggingFace under the NOSIBLE org; signals feed NOSIBLE Search Feeds ("web-scale surveillance") for aspect-based sentiment analysis.

### 2. ARCHITECTURE

1. **Data sampling** — sample a Search Feed of financial news from the NOSIBLE index; real-world, messy, varied snippets (their variety is deliberate — forces robust patterns over memorized artifacts).
2. **Step 1: Look at your data** — hand-label 200 uniformly sampled texts (negative/neutral/positive); study ambiguity and class balance; oversample under-represented classes (they needed more negatives). Hand-labeled set kept separate from the LLM-labeled set.
3. **Step 2: LLM ensemble labeling** — unambiguous decision-tree prompt (full prompts for all three tasks disclosed verbatim); 8 LLMs each label every text; **majority vote** produces the label. Prompt validated first against the 200 hand labels; disagreements + LLM rationales drive prompt refinement (e.g., discovered earnings reports mislabeled neutral → emphasized financial materiality over tone). Then scale 200 → 10,000 → 100,000 samples. Data shape evolution: (200,1) text → (200,2) +human_label → (10,000,9) 8 LLM label columns → (10,000,10) +majority_vote.
4. **Step 3: Baseline classifiers** — embed texts with 6 embedding models (via OpenRouter, embeddings memoized to .npy); train linear `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=0.00001)` per embedding; 80/20 train/val split (pre-shuffled, subscript split); target mapping {0: neutral, 1: positive, −1: negative}. Baseline confirms signal, label quality, and gives a benchmark. Scaling to 100k added 1–2% accuracy. Baseline: 86.65% train / 85.93% val (20,000 val samples).
5. **Step 4: Active-learning relabeling loop** — (a) find rows where ALL linear models agree with each other but DISAGREE with the majority-vote label; (b) consult oracle GPT-5.1 (prompt disclosed: given the labeling prompt + the linear models' consensus prediction, oracle returns `{"correct": true/false, "label": ..., "reason": ...}`); (c) relabel if oracle sides with the baselines, else keep; (d) drop the worst-performing linear model (on val) from the ensemble each iteration; (e) retrain and repeat until no new disagreements. Result: +3.38% train (→90.03%), +3.55% val (→89.48%). Final dataset reached "iter_18" (`financial_sentiment_100.0k_iter_18.ipc`).
6. **Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B** — classification as next-token prediction: chat-templated prompt (system: "Classify the financial sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral."; user: text; assistant target: label + `<|im_end|>`); label masking (−100 on prompt tokens); left-padding; EOS excluded from metrics; monitor train/val loss and PhraseBank accuracy during training. Candidates tested: ModernBERT, DeBERTa, several causal LLMs — Qwen3-0.6B won.
7. **Evaluation** — vs FinBERT (`ProsusAI/finbert` via HF Trainer, macro-F1 + accuracy) and vs zero-shot frontier LLMs, on (a) Financial PhraseBank (4,840 expert-labeled snippets, Malo et al. 2014 — "fake news"/contrived) and (b) the 20% held-out real-world validation set; plus accuracy-vs-cost frontier plots.
8. **Serving** — HF Inference Endpoints, SGLang engine on an L40S GPU; OpenAI-compatible client with `temperature=0, max_tokens=1, logprobs=True, top_logprobs=3`, regex-constrained decoding `"(positive|neutral|negative)"`, `enable_thinking: False`; logprobs → per-label confidence via `math.exp(logprob)`.

### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS

**Headline numbers:**
- 87.34% accuracy on real-world data; 86.4% on Financial PhraseBank; beats FinBERT on both; matches GPT-5.1 accuracy; GPT-5.1 topped it "by a margin" on the benchmark but is orders of magnitude more expensive.
- Baseline linear model: 86.65% train / 85.93% val → after relabeling 90.03% / 89.48% (+3.38 / +3.55). "~3.5% validation accuracy improvement as a result of relabeling."
- 100,000-sample dataset; 20,000 validation samples (80/20).

**Labeler ensemble (8 models, via OpenRouter):** xAI Grok 4 Fast; Grok 4 Fast (reasoning enabled); Google Gemini 2.5 Flash; OpenAI GPT-5 Nano; OpenAI GPT-4.1 Mini; OpenAI gpt-oss-120b; Meta Llama 4 Maverick; Qwen Qwen3 32B. Aggregation = majority vote.

**Embedding ensemble (6 models, via OpenRouter):** Qwen3-Embedding-8B; Qwen3-Embedding-4B; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; OpenAI Text-Embedding-3-Large; Google Gemini-Embedding-001; Mistral-Embed-2312. (Usage volume put NOSIBLE 2nd on the OpenRouter embeddings leaderboard for Qwen3-Embedding-8B, expected 1st once operationalized.)

**Baseline classifier:** `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=0.00001)`; labels {positive:1, neutral:0, negative:−1}; polars DataFrames; embeddings cached as .npy; confusion matrices computed per split.

**Oracle:** OpenAI GPT-5.1 via OpenRouter. Oracle prompt embeds the original labeling prompt as the user message and asks in the system message whether the baseline-consensus label is correct, returning JSON `{"correct": "true"|"false", "label": <one of labels>, "reason": ...}` (ends with "P.S. Think fast there is no time to waste.").

**Prompts (all three disclosed verbatim in post — key properties):**
- Sentiment: negative/neutral/positive defined via *material impact* on financial performance, share price, reputation, or outlook; materiality note enumerates share price, revenue, costs, profitability, cash flow, guidance, regulatory exposure, reputation, risk exposure, competitive position; explicit ASCII decision tree (check clearly-negative → clearly-positive → else neutral); conflicting sentiment → pick dominant, else neutral; JSON output `{"rationale", "financial_sentiment"}`; default-to-neutral instruction.
- Forward-looking: classify main event's temporal orientation "forward" | "not-forward"; disambiguation rules: ignore reporting-verb tense; plans/intentions/targets/guidance = forward even if approved in past ("Board approved new product launch" → forward); when in doubt → not-forward; JSON `{"tense", "rationale"}`.
- Prediction: "predictive" | "not-predictive"; predictive = concrete claim/forecast/estimate about a specific event; numerical estimates about current or future stats = predictive; analyst estimates/ratings predictive even in past tense; plans/hopes/schedules/retrospectives = not-predictive; default not-predictive; JSON `{"rationale", "causal"}`.

**Fine-tuning setup (full script disclosed):**
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` (600M params; "run it on a phone"; not hosted on OpenRouter). Alternatives tested: ModernBERT, DeBERTa, several causal LLMs.
- Approach cites Qwen3Guard (arXiv 2510.14276) "Guard approach" — classification as next-token prediction, no classification head; representation is the tokenized text directly (not embeddings).
- Tokenization: `apply_chat_template(..., add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False)`; answer = `f"{label}<|im_end|>"`; `assert len(answer_tokens)==2` (label must be a single token + EOS); truncate at 2048 tokens.
- Label masking: `labels = [-100] * len(prompt_tokens["input_ids"]) + answer_tokens["input_ids"]` — loss only on label+EOS tokens ("forces the model to learn classification, not memorize prompts").
- Left padding: `tokenizer.padding_side = "left"`; `pad_token = eos_token` if missing; `trust_remote_code=True` ("essential for Qwen3"). Right-padding "breaks everything" for causal batched prediction.
- Model load: `torch.bfloat16`, `device_map="auto"`.
- TrainingArguments: `gradient_accumulation_steps=4`, `per_device_train_batch_size=16`, `per_device_eval_batch_size=16`, `num_train_epochs=5`, `learning_rate=2e-5`, `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `warmup_ratio=0.03`, `max_grad_norm=1.0`, `weight_decay=0.1`, `neftune_noise_alpha=5`, `bf16=True`, `optim="adamw_torch_fused"`, `group_by_length=True`, `torch_compile=False`, `eval_strategy="steps"`, `eval_steps=500`, `save_steps=500`, `save_total_limit=3`, `load_best_model_at_end=True`, `metric_for_best_model="eval_val_loss"`, `logging_steps=10`, `logging_first_step=True`, `report_to="none"`.
- Eval sets during training: 5% of train, the 20% val split, and Financial PhraseBank; collator `DataCollatorForSeq2Seq(padding=True)`; `num_proc=8` for tokenization.
- Metric pitfall (disclosed bug): including EOS tokens in accuracy gave "suspiciously good results"; fix = mask both −100 and `<|im_end|>` token id (`compute_metrics_without_eos`: shift preds `[:, :-1]` vs labels `[:, 1:]`, `valid_mask = (labels != -100) & (labels != eos_token_id)`, macro-F1 + accuracy); `preprocess_logits_for_metrics` argmaxes logits (Batch, Seq, Vocab) → (Batch, Seq) to save memory. Verified true accuracy after training on an out-of-sample dataset.
- Data files: `financial_sentiment_100.0k_iter_18.ipc` (polars IPC), `financial_phrase_bank.ndjson`; workspace `/workspace/.nosible`; `train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42)`.
- FinBERT eval: `ProsusAI/finbert`, label2id {positive:0, negative:1, neutral:2}, max_length 512, eval batch 32, macro-F1 preferred.

**Benchmarks/eval sets:**
- Financial PhraseBank: 4,840 snippets, human-expert labeled, Malo et al. (2014) — characterized as contrived/"fake news"; FinBERT does well here but "sucks on real-world data" (overfit to cleaner benchmark data).
- Real-world eval: held-out 20% of the 100k NOSIBLE dataset ("real news").

**Cost methodology (disclosed):**
- LLMs: input+output token cost per million summed in a **10:1 input:output ratio** (typical for the labeling prompt).
- Fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B: estimated at a conservative **100:1 ratio** (output = label token + EOS only).

**Serving recipe (disclosed):** HF Inference Endpoints → Deploy → HF Inference Endpoints; hardware "a beefy GPU like a L40S"; engine SGLang with Max Prefill Tokens 65536; container args `--dtype float16 --cuda-graph-max-bs 128 --disable-radix-cache`; Download Pattern "Download Everything". Client: OpenAI SDK, `temperature=0`, `max_tokens=1`, `logprobs=True`, `top_logprobs=len(labels)`, `extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, "regex": "(positive|neutral|negative)"}`; confidence = `math.exp(lp.logprob)` per label token. Key insight: "causal models aren't just for text generation" — logprobs make them production-ready classifiers.

**Open-sourced artifacts (HF):** datasets `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` (100k cleaned/deduped/labeled), `NOSIBLE/forward-looking`, `NOSIBLE/prediction`; models `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment-v1.1-base`, `NOSIBLE/forward-looking-v1.2-base`, `NOSIBLE/prediction-v1.1-base`.

**Citations:** FinBERT (Araci 2019, arXiv 1908.10063); Financial PhraseBank (Malo et al. 2014; HF `takala/financial_phrasebank`); Qwen3 Technical Report (arXiv 2505.09388); Qwen3Guard Technical Report (arXiv 2510.14276).

### 4. BUILD RECIPE (educational scale)

1. Gather 1k–10k real-world financial text snippets (mix polished earnings prose with noisy consumer/off-topic text — the variety is deliberate). [disclosed principle; inferred source — use RSS/news APIs or the released `NOSIBLE/financial-sentiment` dataset directly]
2. Hand-label 200 uniform samples as negative/neutral/positive; note ambiguity patterns and class balance; oversample scarce classes (negatives). Keep this set held out. [disclosed]
3. Write a decision-tree labeling prompt with domain definitions, materiality note, disambiguation rules, default-to-neutral fallback, and JSON-only output — or reuse the verbatim prompts from the post. [disclosed]
4. Label the full set with 3–8 cheap API LLMs (post used 8 via OpenRouter); take majority vote; validate against the 200 hand labels; refine prompt from disagreements + rationales. [disclosed; inferred that 3–5 labelers suffice at educational scale]
5. Embed all texts with 2–6 embedding models (post: Qwen3-Embedding family, text-embedding-3-large, gemini-embedding-001, mistral-embed; educationally, local sentence-transformers work); cache embeddings to .npy. [disclosed; inferred local-model substitution]
6. Train one `SGDClassifier(loss='hinge', penalty='l2', alpha=1e-5)` per embedding, 80/20 split; check train≈val accuracy (no overfit) and that accuracy beats chance (signal exists). [disclosed — code given]
7. Active-learning loop: find rows where all linear models agree but the majority vote disagrees → ask an oracle LLM (post: GPT-5.1; any strong model works) with the disclosed oracle prompt → relabel when oracle sides with baselines → drop worst linear model on val → retrain → repeat to convergence (post took ~18 iterations). [disclosed; inferred oracle substitution]
8. Fine-tune `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` with the disclosed script: chat template (system instruction + text + assistant label), label masking (−100 on prompt), left padding, single-token label + `<|im_end|>`, bf16, lr 2e-5 cosine, 5 epochs, batch 16 × grad-accum 4, neftune 5, weight decay 0.1, best-model-on-val-loss. [disclosed — full hyperparameters given]
9. Evaluate with the EOS-excluded token metric (mask −100 AND eos id) on val + Financial PhraseBank (`takala/financial_phrasebank` on HF); compare against `ProsusAI/finbert` and one or two zero-shot API LLMs with the same labeling prompt; verify on an out-of-sample set. [disclosed]
10. Serve with regex-constrained single-token decoding (`max_tokens=1`, regex `(positive|neutral|negative)`, thinking disabled) and read logprobs for calibrated confidence — via SGLang/vLLM on GPU, or plain `transformers` generation at toy scale. [disclosed serving config; inferred that local transformers/ONNX inference is an acceptable educational stand-in for the L40S/SGLang endpoint]
11. Optional: repeat the whole pipeline for the forward-looking and prediction binary tasks using the two other disclosed prompts. [disclosed]

### 5. GAPS

- Chart-only numbers: the PhraseBank and real-world accuracy figures for every compared LLM/FinBERT, and the actual dollar costs on the cost-vs-accuracy plots, are images — only 87.34%, 86.4%, and the baseline/relabeling numbers appear in text.
- How ModernBERT/DeBERTa/other causal candidates scored (why exactly Qwen3-0.6B won) — no comparison numbers given.
- How the raw Search Feed was sampled/filtered (query, dedup, date range, per-company balance) and how negatives were oversampled — proprietary pipeline.
- Exact number of relabeled samples per iteration, total relabeled count, and total iterations (only inferable as ~18 from the filename `iter_18`).
- Which/how many linear models remained at convergence after the drop-worst rule.
- Fine-tuning hardware, wall-clock time, and training cost are unstated (only the `/workspace` path hints at a rented GPU box).
- Production throughput/latency numbers for the served Qwen3-0.6B (only "orders of magnitude" cheaper/faster claims and the 100:1 cost-ratio estimate).
- Tie-breaking rule for the 8-model majority vote (8 is even; 3-class ties possible) is not specified.
- The `embed_data()` helper (OpenRouter embedding calls) is referenced but not shown.

## Cross-Post Synthesis (for the replica build guide)

The three posts form one evolving pattern, each stage a drop-in upgrade of the last:

| Dimension | Post 1 (2024-01) | Post 2 (2024-02) | Post 3 (2025-12) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Role | Benchmark + label source selection | Ensemble teacher + linear distillation | LLM-labeled + active learning + causal-LM fine-tune |
| Labelers | 12+ individual models | 5-member summed ensemble (90.4% human agreement) | 8-LLM majority vote + GPT-5.1 oracle relabeling |
| Student | — | OLS on sentence-transformer embeddings (80.4%) | Fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B next-token classifier (87.3% real-world) |
| Ensemble rule | — | greedy iterative addition, sum, threshold ±1 | majority vote; drop-worst baseline pruning |
| Key metric | agreement with 250 human labels | OOS agreement with teacher (75/25 split, seed 42) | accuracy/macro-F1 on 20% holdout + PhraseBank, EOS-excluded |
| Cost story | $0.00983/story GPT-4; $92k/10M | ~$0 marginal; 0.005 s/story; <1 compute-day/10M | 100:1 vs 10:1 token-ratio cost model; L40S + SGLang |

An educational replica (cybernaut_mini-style) can implement all three stages against one small corpus: Stage A = multi-model labeling + agreement matrix (Post 1), Stage B = iterative-addition teacher + OLS students (Post 2), Stage C = active-learning relabel loop + Qwen3-0.6B fine-tune with label masking and regex-constrained serving (Post 3). Every load-bearing formula, prompt, and hyperparameter needed is quoted above; the main unavoidable substitutions are the news corpus itself and the retired 2023-era LLMs (PaLM-2 Bison/Unicorn, GPT-4-Original).

The universal design pattern: **share of breadth-weighted publisher attention matching a concept, normalized by a corpus-growth-robust denominator**.

13	## Post 1 — "We Rebuilt the Geopolitical Risk Index with Nosible World"
14	
15	### 1. WHAT IT IS
16	
17	A replication of the Federal Reserve Geopolitical Risk (GPR) index — both the original Caldara & Iacoviello (2018/2022) keyword-count version and the newer AI-GPR (Iacoviello & Tong, 2026) LLM-scored version — built purely from metadata already attached to NOSIBLE's de-duplicated multilingual event database: IPTC topic tags, NER country entities, publisher breadth, and (for two gap-filling extensions) stored embeddings. It solves the problem that "geopolitical risk is a feeling, not a figure": producing a live daily/monthly numeric risk series (global, per-country, per-country-pair, and oil-supply) that quant/risk models can consume, with no LLM reading each article and no keyword lists — matching the published benchmarks at correlations of ~0.90–0.99.
18	
19	### 2. ARCHITECTURE
20	
21	1. **Event store (input)** — NOSIBLE World database, 2010–present; study window 2019+ (overlap with published indices), 13.2M de-duplicated events. Each event: IPTC 3-level topic, main country, `ent_gpe` NER entities, `total_netlocs` breadth, `oai_vector` embedding, date.
22	2. **Geopolitical classifier (rule filter)** — exact match on IPTC ontology *codes* (never label words):
23	   - `iptc_level_1 == "conflict, war and peace"` OR
24	   - `iptc_level_2 == "international relations"` OR
25	   - `iptc_level_3 in {"war crime", "genocide", "terrorism", "nuclear policy"}`
26	3. **Global index aggregation** — per day, breadth-weighted share: sum of `total_netlocs` over geopolitical events ÷ sum over all events. One group-by over the event table.
27	4. **Detrending variant** — same numerator; denominator swapped to a trailing 12-month average of total attention (removes corpus-growth drift). This detrended version is carried through the rest of the post.
28	5. **Rescaling (display only)** — each series rescaled to average 100 over 2020–2024; correlations unchanged.
29	6. **Country attribution layer** — resolve `ent_gpe` entity strings to countries (whole-string, case-insensitive match against a table of country names, official aliases, nationalities ≥4 letters, native-language names; partial matches rejected; ambiguous strings like bare "Georgia" dropped). Attribution set = main country + all resolved NER countries. Explode events to attribution sets → group by (country, month) → divide by global denominator `B(m)` = trailing 12-month average of total monthly breadth.
30	7. **Bilateral (pair) layer** — self-join each event's attribution set into unordered pairs → group by (pair, month) → same `B(m)`.
31	8. **Embedding rescue path #1 (trade coercion)** — one anchor phrase embedded; event admitted if `geopolitical(e) OR cosine(event, anchor) >= 0.40`. Fixes the China–USA gap (tariff events are IPTC "international trade", economy branch).
32	9. **Embedding rescue path #2 (Oil-GPR)** — three oil-supply anchor phrases; `relevance(e)` = max cosine; keep events that are geopolitical AND `relevance(e) >= 0.30`; weight by `relevance(e) × breadth(e)`; divide by `B(m)`. Per-region versions attribute surviving events to producer regions/countries as in step 6.
33	10. **Validation** — Pearson correlation vs published GPR / AI-GPR series, on levels and month-over-month changes; z-scored per-region charts for oil.

35	### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS
36	
37	**Benchmarks & context**
38	- Original GPR (Caldara & Iacoviello 2018; AER 112(4), 2022): counts geopolitical-risk words across **ten major newspapers**, as a share of all articles; reaches back over a century. Data at matteoiacoviello.com/gpr.htm.
39	- AI-GPR (Iacoviello & Tong 2026): an LLM scores each article's geopolitical risk **from zero to one**; adds per-country, per-pair, and oil-supply cuts. This is the target NOSIBLE holds itself to.
40	- Institutional users named: Federal Reserve (maintains it), IMF GFSR April 2025 Ch.2 and WEO April 2026 Ch.1, ECB/ESRB January 2026 fragmentation report.
41	- The two published versions agree with each other "at about the same level" as NOSIBLE reaches.
42	
43	**Data**
44	- Database covers 2010–today; study uses 2019 onward; **13.2 million de-duplicated events**.
45	- One real event = one record regardless of outlet count; `total_netlocs` = distinct publisher count = `breadth(e)`.
46	- Multilingual; no per-article LLM pass; no keyword list.
47	
48	**Geopolitical filter (verbatim)**
49	```
50	geopolitical(e) is TRUE when ANY of these hold:
51	    iptc_level_1 == "conflict, war and peace"
52	    iptc_level_2 == "international relations"
53	    iptc_level_3 in { "war crime", "genocide", "terrorism", "nuclear policy" }
54	```
55	- Matched on ontology codes exactly, never label words ("weather warning", "tug-of-war" cannot leak in).
56	- IPTC Media Topics: structured three-level hierarchy; top-level buckets include `conflict, war and peace`, `economy, business and finance`, `health`.

129	## Post 2 — "Turning News into a Risk-On/Risk-Off Equity Signal"
130	
131	### 1. WHAT IT IS
132	
133	A daily market-stress gauge built by scoring every de-duplicated news event's stored embedding against 17 fixed "market stress" anchor phrases, converting the breadth-weighted share of stressful attention into a strictly-trailing robust z-score, and driving a two-state (equities vs T-bills) overlay strategy from it. Problem solved: turning qualitative news flow into a causal, tradeable risk-off trigger. On the S&P 500 over an untouched 2015–2026 test window the overlay keeps ~buy-and-hold's total return (+254% vs +269%) while cutting max drawdown from −34% to −18% and raising Sharpe from 0.64 to 0.89; the identical frozen rule transfers to the Nasdaq and Russell 2000. The post explicitly claims full reproducibility from the disclosed parameters plus the event database and EODHD prices. "The point is risk, not return."
134	
135	### 2. ARCHITECTURE
136	
137	1. **Inputs** — per de-duplicated event: `oai_vector` (`text-embedding-3-large`), `total_netlocs`, date; full daily history.
138	2. **Anchor bank** — 17 short stress concepts, each embedded once with the same model; entity- and time-agnostic (no specific countries, crises, or dates) so no hindsight enters the backtest.
139	3. **Dimensionality** — truncate both event vectors and anchors to the **first 1024 of 3,072 Matryoshka dims**, then **L2-renormalise**.
140	4. **Per-event scoring** — `relevance(e)` = max cosine over the 17 anchors; event counts only if `relevance(e) >= 0.30`.
141	5. **Daily intensity** — Σ `relevance(e)·breadth(e)` over qualifying events ÷ Σ `breadth(e)` over ALL events that day.
142	6. **Causal calibration** — (a) 7-day trailing mean; (b) robust z with trailing 252-trading-day median and MAD × 1.4826; (c) EWMA span 7. None uses future data.
143	7. **Lag & execution** — signal lagged 2 trading days before it can trigger; positions execute on the next bar.
144	8. **Two-state rule** — LONG equities; exit to `BIL.US` when z > 1.75; re-enter when out ≥ 5 days AND z < 0.25; cost 1 bp × |Δweight| per position change.
145	9. **Selection harness** — grid sweep on 2010–2013 train window only, objective = Sortino improvement over buy-and-hold, one-year (252-day) embargo, plateau selection (median of top-20% cells), then frozen.
146	10. **Validation** — sanity overlay vs VIX (not part of strategy); backtests on GSPC, IXIC, IWM with EODHD adjusted closes, daily log returns.
147	
148	### 3. CONCRETE TECHNICAL FACTS
149	
150	**The 17 anchors (verbatim, name → phrase)**
151	```
152	credit_spreads     Widening corporate credit spreads, surging default risk and stress in corporate bond markets
153	liquidity          A liquidity crisis or funding stress freezing financial markets
154	deleveraging       Forced selling, margin calls, deleveraging and liquidations cascading through markets
155	recession          Rising fears of recession, sharp economic slowdown or collapsing growth
156	banking_credit     A banking crisis, credit crunch, defaults or financial-system instability
157	volatility_fear    A surge in financial market volatility, fear, panic and investor anxiety
158	equity_selloff     A sharp sell-off, crash or plunge in global stock markets
159	flight_to_safety   A flight to safety and risk-off panic: investors dumping risky assets for government bonds, gold and reserve currencies
160	sovereign_fx       A sovereign-debt default or currency crisis destabilising markets
161	monetary_shock     An unexpected hawkish central bank or interest-rate shock tightening financial conditions
162	rates_turmoil      Turmoil in government bond markets: a bond rout, spiking yields and surging interest-rate volatility
163	tail_hedging       Investors rushing to buy downside protection and hedge against a market crash; spiking demand for portfolio insurance
164	earnings_distress  A wave of corporate profit warnings, earnings misses, bankruptcies and corporate distress

166	tariffs            New import tariffs, escalating protectionism and a trade war between major economies

171	**Signal math (verbatim)**
172	```
173	intensity(t) = Σ over events on day t with relevance(e) ≥ 0.30 of relevance(e)·breadth(e)
174	               ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
175	               Σ over all events on day t of breadth(e)
176	```
177	- Embedding: 3,072-d `text-embedding-3-large`; first 1024 dims kept (Matryoshka training makes the prefix a complete embedding), L2-renormalised.
178	- Share not count → immune to crawl-volume drift; breadth as weight → a 200-outlet story counts once, weighted by 200.
179	- Relevance scores pile up near zero (most news is not about market stress). Example qualifying headlines: 0.57 → `tariffs` ("Trump Tariff Threats on Greenland Spark Global Trade War Fears"); 0.45 → `employment_shock` ("US Jobless Claims Rise Marginally While Q3 Productivity Surges").

181	**Calibration (verbatim)**
182	```
183	1. s(t) = 7-day trailing mean of intensity(t)              (settle daily noise)
184	2. z(t) = (s(t) - median) / (1.4826 * MAD)                 (median and MAD over the trailing
185	                                                            252 trading days; 1.4826 puts it
186	                                                            in sigma units)
187	3. z(t) = EWMA(z, span = 7)                                (so the position does not flicker)
188	```
189	
190	**Trading rule (verbatim)**
191	```
192	state = LONG (fully in equities)
193	  if state == LONG and z > 1.75:          -> OUT (move to BIL.US), days_out = 0
194	  if state == OUT:
195	      days_out += 1
196	      if days_out >= 5 and z < 0.25:      -> LONG
197	cost = 1 bp charged on |w(t) - w(t-1)| each time the position changes
198	```
199	- News lagged **2 trading days**; execution next bar. Defensive leg `BIL.US` (SPDR 1-3 Month T-Bill ETF); overlay earns equity return when long, T-bill return when out.

204	- Objective: **Sortino improvement over buy-and-hold** (improvement, not raw level, so the choice rewards timing rather than equity exposure).
205	- Plateau not peak: take top 20% of cells by train score; set each parameter to the grid value nearest that set's median. Frozen result: exit 1.75 / enter 0.25 / hold 5.
206	- Full frozen parameter set (verbatim): relevance floor 0.30, rolling-mean window 7, robust-z window 252, EWMA span 7, news lag 2 trading days, exit z 1.75, enter z 0.25, min hold 5 days, 1 bp/turn, defensive leg BIL.US.

249	## Post 3 — "An Embedding-Based Approach to Trade and Economic Policy Uncertainty"
250	
251	### 1. WHAT IT IS
252	
253	A reconstruction of two canonical keyword-count policy-uncertainty indices — the Fed's Trade Policy Uncertainty (TPU) index (Caldara, Iacoviello, Molligo, Prestipino & Raffo, *Journal of Monetary Economics* 2020) and Baker-Bloom-Davis's Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index (*QJE* 2016), plus two EPU category indices (national security, healthcare) — using only cosine similarity between stored event embeddings and small hand-written anchor-sentence sets: 5 sentences for TPU, 60 for the EPU family. The keyword papers' "topic word AND uncertainty word" rule becomes a topic-relevance gate plus a **signed** uncertainty weight from an uncertain-vs-certain sentence pair via `tanh` of the similarity gap — giving the replica a directional resolved↔uncertain axis the published indices lack. Scoring 14.9M events (2015–2026) takes ~12 minutes on a laptop; TPU matches the published benchmark at 0.87 monthly levels / 0.82 monthly changes (the two official indices agree at 0.96 / 0.70 with each other), and EPU matches the published US series at 0.77 on monthly levels.
254	
255	### 2. ARCHITECTURE
256	
257	1. **Inputs** — per event: `oai_vector` (`text-embedding-3-large`, 3,072-d; first 1,024 kept via Matryoshka, L2-normalized "so cosine similarities stay meaningful"), `total_netlocs` breadth, date (day its coverage peaked), primary-country tag (for the US-only EPU).
258	2. **TPU anchor set** — 3 topic sentences (tariffs, agreements, disputes) + 2 axis sentences (uncertain, certain).
259	3. **Relevance gate** — `relevant(e) = max cosine(event, 3 topic phrases) >= 0.35`.
260	4. **Polarity/weight** — `polarity(e) = tanh((uncertain_sim − certain_sim)/0.1)` ∈ [−1, +1]; `w_unc(e) = (1 + polarity)/2` ∈ [0, 1].
261	5. **Daily index** — Σ `breadth(e)·w_unc(e)` over relevant events ÷ trailing 12-month average of total daily breadth (worldwide events, every language, for TPU — not a US subset).
262	6. **Net-polarity diagnostic** — breadth-weighted mean polarity over relevant events per day, with a state-dependent asymmetric smoother (fast 3-day half-life when polarity jumps ≥1.5σ above its trailing year with no look-ahead; slow 30-day half-life on calm days and moves toward resolution).
263	7. **EPU extension** — 10 policy "levers" (monetary policy, taxes, spending, debt and shutdowns, entitlements, regulation, financial regulation, trade, major economic laws, shutting down/reopening the economy), each a set of matched uncertain/certain sentence pairs; 60 sentences total. Lever score = max of its two framings; relevance = max over all levers ≥ 0.35; polarity from the best-matching pair. US-only numerator (US-attributed policy-relevant events) and denominator (trailing 12-month average of total US-attributed monthly breadth).
264	8. **Category indices** — national security & healthcare: event must additionally score ≥ **0.25** against that category's own sentence pairs (matching the paper's category definition).
265	9. **Validation** — monthly/quarterly Pearson correlations (levels and changes) vs published TPU, BBD trade EPU, published US EPU and categorical series, on 2015-03–2026-05 monthly, jointly non-null rows, each series rebased to its own mean; episode-rank checks (out of 135 months); lead-lag check vs the realized US tariff rate (BEA NIPA customs duties ÷ goods imports, via DBnomics).
266
